name: Digitaria

project_scope.note: Only the two installed taxa, not a complete county Digitaria flora. D. ciliaris introduced; D. cognata native to Texas, but native-by-county audit not performed or changed.

look_here_first: FIRST LOOK AT SEEDHEAD ARCHITECTURE: tight, near-fingerlike one-sided RACEMES with PAIRED spikelets = likely southern crabgrass; airy diffuse BROOM/TUMBLEWEED panicle with hairy swollen branch axils and separate terminal spikelets = likely fall witchgrass. THEN check ligule, leaf edge, basal growth form and mature florets.

recognition.where_to_look_first: Is the flowering head a small clutch of straight fingerlike branches or a wide fluffy cloud? With hand lens examine where spikelets attach and count heads. Photograph collar, leaf-base and whole rooted clump.
priority: spikelets paired along one side of raceme versus solitary along delicate panicle ends
swollen hairy branch axils present or absent
wavy pale leaf edge versus mostly straight margin
annual rooted prostrate nodes versus perennial horizontal crown
membranous true ligule and sterile lemma nerves

comparison_lesson.memory_rule: FINGERS AND PAIRS = CILIARIS; AIRY TUMBLING BROOM AND HAIRY NODES = COGNATA.
quick_split: D. ciliaris / southern crabgrass: low spreading annual, several fingerlike one-sided racemes bearing pairs of spikelets; transparent membranous collar ligule; compare large crabgrass sterile-lemma nerve prickles.
D. cognata / fall witchgrass: wiry perennial, large highly diffuse seedhead that may blow away, fuzzy spikelets, hairy swollen panicle branch nodes and distinctive whitish crimped blade edge.
closeouts: D. sanguinalis vs D. ciliaris is a technical Digitaria split requiring mature sterile-lemma nerve inspection; never call by head color alone.
D. cognata = Leptoloma cognatum in older field guides; do not duplicate its canonical record.
Other Digitaria species in Central Texas are NOT represented by this two-species key; mark unresolved examples as Digitaria sp.

comparison_matrix.title: Digitaria — southern crabgrass versus fall witchgrass
rows: Rooted crown and repeated seasonal observation
Wiry stems from horizontal often hairy base
Photograph whole base, not just seedhead
Diffuse airy broom, broad open branches
Pairs along rachis nodes, stalk lengths uneven
Tiny hairy spikelets at end portions of fine branches
Often swollen with conspicuous radiating white hairs
Relatively broad in TX treatment, margins not diagnostic alone
Typically shorter narrow blade, whitish crinkled edge
Must check collar; no stand-in from panicle photo
D. sanguinalis sterile-lemma nerves; Eleusine crown/rows

Whole southern crabgrass rooted runner plus opposite full fall witchgrass clump.
Southern crabgrass raceme-side paired spikelets and true membranous ligule close-up.
Fall witchgrass radiating axil hairs, wavy white blade edge and terminal fuzzy spikelet close-up.
Technical comparison: D. ciliaris vs D. sanguinalis lateral nerves on sterile lemmas at sufficient magnification.
what_to_teach_crew: An open-panicle Digitaria is not necessarily the common crabgrass; both of these belong to the same genus.
One-sided fingerlike branches bearing spikelets in PAIRS are the first southern crabgrass clue.
For fall witchgrass, examine the airy broom, look for radiating long hairs at swollen branch axils, and run a finger along the crinkled pale leaf edge.
Photograph the whole plant, one entire seedhead, the ligule, and an actual mature spikelet, preferably the same individual.
For native habitat assessments, don't confuse the introduced southern crabgrass with Texas-native fall witchgrass, and don't infer Hays County nativity from a Texas-level reference.
